key_insight: Early three-dimensionality in transonic shock–boundary-layer interactions is governed mainly by viscous and compressibility effects, while vortex stretching becomes intermittently appreciable with shock-induced separation.
engineering_relevance: Understanding when three-dimensional effects emerge can help assess the limits of two-dimensional aerodynamic predictions for natural laminar flow airfoils.
method: High-fidelity 3D simulations of the SHM1 airfoil in normal-shock onset, drag-divergence, and shock-induced-separation regimes.
Comparison of spanwise-averaged 3D surface pressure and skin friction with prior 2D simulations.
Analysis of streamwise and wall-normal enstrophy evolution and compressible enstrophy transport budgets.
evidence_signal: Across three operating conditions, the simulations identify an initial interval of close 2D–3D agreement followed by departures, with the same principal enstrophy mechanisms contributing differently across SBLI topologies.
watch_item: The study addresses short-time evolution on one airfoil; long-time behavior and generalization to other geometries remain unestablished by the abstract.
paper_title: Onset of three dimensionality in transonic shock boundary layer interaction over a natural laminar flow airfoil
